trials.title: Embedding Formative Assessment
trials.subtitle: A project to test a professional development programme, which enables schools to embed formative assessment practices.

sections.heading: EEF Summary
sections.text: The programme builds on existing evidence that formative assessment can improve students’ learning. Many schools already prioritise formative assessment, but often report that it can be challenging to implement. EEF funded this evaluation as it offers a scalable approach to supporting schools to deliver the approach.Students in the Embedding Formative Assessment schools made the equivalent of two months’ additional progress, with attainment measured using Attainment 8 GCSE scores. This result has a very high security rating.The headline finding, combined with further analyses and the implementation and process evaluation, provides good evidence of the effectiveness of Embedding Formative Assessment. EEF will now explore how to support more schools to use the programme.
sections.html:
The programme builds on existing evidence that formative assessment can improve students’ learning. Many schools already prioritise formative assessment, but often report that it can be challenging to implement. EEF funded this evaluation as it offers a scalable approach to supporting schools to deliver the approach.

Students in the Embedding Formative Assessment schools made the equivalent of two months’ additional progress, with attainment measured using Attainment 8 GCSE scores. This result has a very high security rating.

The headline finding, combined with further analyses and the implementation and process evaluation, provides good evidence of the effectiveness of Embedding Formative Assessment. EEF will now explore how to support more schools to use the programme.

sections.heading: Evaluation Conclusions
sections.text: Students in the Embedding Formative Assessment schools made the equivalent of two additional months’ progress in their Attainment 8 GCSE score, using the standard EEF conversion from pupil scores to months progress. This result has a very high security rating.The project found no evidence that Embedding Formative Assessment improved English or Maths GCSE attainment specifically.The additional progress made by children in the lowest third for prior attainment was greater than that made by children in the highest third. These results are less robust and have a lower security rating than the overall findings because of the smaller number of pupils.Teachers were positive about the Teacher Learning Communities. They felt that these improved their practice by allowing valuable dialogue between teachers, and encouraged experimentation with formative assessment strategies.The process evaluation indicated it may take more time for improvements in teaching practices and pupil learning strategies to feed fully into pupil attainment. Many teachers thought that younger students were more receptive to the intervention than their older and more exam-minded peers.
sections.html:
1. Students in the Embedding Formative Assessment schools made the equivalent of two additional months’ progress in their Attainment 8 GCSE score, using the standard EEF conversion from pupil scores to months progress. This result has a very high security rating.
  2. The project found no evidence that Embedding Formative Assessment improved English or Maths GCSE attainment specifically.
  3. The additional progress made by children in the lowest third for prior attainment was greater than that made by children in the highest third. These results are less robust and have a lower security rating than the overall findings because of the smaller number of pupils.
  4. Teachers were positive about the Teacher Learning Communities. They felt that these improved their practice by allowing valuable dialogue between teachers, and encouraged experimentation with formative assessment strategies.
  5. The process evaluation indicated it may take more time for improvements in teaching practices and pupil learning strategies to feed fully into pupil attainment. Many teachers thought that younger students were more receptive to the intervention than their older and more exam-minded peers.

trials.title: Embedding Formative Assessment – scale up evaluation
trials.subtitle: This two-year programme aims to improve secondary school pupil outcomes by embedding the use of formative assessment strategies across a school.

sections.heading: EEF Summary
sections.text: The programme was developed based on existing evidence that formative assessment can improve students’ learning. Many schools already prioritise formative assessment, but often report that it can be challenging to implement. EFA provides schools with a structured approach to developing their formative assessment practices. A previous EEF effectiveness trial in 140 schools had promising results, with students in the EFA schools making the equivalent of two months’ additional progress on their Attainment 8 GCSE scores. The result of this trial had a very high security rating. As a result of the promising effectiveness trial, EEF supported EFA to scale up by subsidising the cost of the programme for schools through the Department for Education’s (DfE) Accelerator Fund, with schools in Education Investment Areas prioritised for access. EEF commissioned a team from the Behavioural Insights Team (BIT) to evaluate the scale-up of the EFA programme over four years (2019−2023). This evaluation assessed several key aspects of implementation to gain insights into how SSAT and EEF can support effective scaling. Key findings include:Significant organisational and programme strategy adjustments were necessary, such as expanding the staff and consultant base, automating processes, and increasing marketing efforts to sustain the scale of operations.SSAT’s monitoring and evaluation framework was vital to understanding and effectively managing the programme’s reach and impact.Post-pandemic, challenges in reach and recruitment emerged as substantial. A new government fund to support catch up enabled a 70% DfE subsidy to encourage participation, resulting in increased recruitment and a participant pool from schools with higher-than-average free school meal (FSM) levels.Implementation fidelity remained high with minimal deviations from the core programme.Contextual factors such as a positive school culture and government support positively influenced adoption and implementation.Sustainability evidence showed that the programme continued to influence school practices after two years, with 56% of teachers noting a change in their general practices.The cost of the program was equivalent to £2.02 per pupil annually.The scale-up was informed by two previous pieces of research. A 2022 mailer trial looked at how different marketing strategies encouraged the adoption of an evidence-based programme by schools. An interim report from the first phase of the research identified that School Leads, TLC Leaders and classroom teachers made a range of adaptations to the programme due to contextual factors including other CPD priorities, the ongoing impact of Covid, the school’s leadership and culture, and specific characteristics of a school’s staff and pupils. The research also identified a lack of data on mentors and systems to ensure that the data collected was acted upon. BIT subsequently worked with SSAT to develop a comprehensive monitoring and evaluation plan and a new set of feedback surveys to support this, which was shown to improve impact management in the final evaluation.
sections.html:
The programme was developed based on existing evidence that formative assessment can improve students’ learning. Many schools already prioritise formative assessment, but often report that it can be challenging to implement. EFA provides schools with a structured approach to developing their formative assessment practices.

A previous EEF effectiveness trial in 140 schools had promising results, with students in the EFA schools making the equivalent of two months’ additional progress on their Attainment 8 GCSE scores. The result of this trial had a very high security rating.

As a result of the promising effectiveness trial, EEF supported EFA to scale up by subsidising the cost of the programme for schools through the Department for Education’s (DfE) Accelerator Fund, with schools in Education Investment Areas prioritised for access.

EEF commissioned a team from the Behavioural Insights Team (BIT) to evaluate the scale-up of the EFA programme over four years (2019−2023). This evaluation assessed several key aspects of implementation to gain insights into how SSAT and EEF can support effective scaling.

Key findings include:

  • Significant organisational and programme strategy adjustments were necessary, such as expanding the staff and consultant base, automating processes, and increasing marketing efforts to sustain the scale of operations.
  • SSAT’s monitoring and evaluation framework was vital to understanding and effectively managing the programme’s reach and impact.
  • Post-pandemic, challenges in reach and recruitment emerged as substantial. A new government fund to support catch up enabled a 70% DfE subsidy to encourage participation, resulting in increased recruitment and a participant pool from schools with higher-than-average free school meal (FSM) levels.
  • Implementation fidelity remained high with minimal deviations from the core programme.
  • Contextual factors such as a positive school culture and government support positively influenced adoption and implementation.
  • Sustainability evidence showed that the programme continued to influence school practices after two years, with 56% of teachers noting a change in their general practices.
  • The cost of the program was equivalent to £2.02 per pupil annually.


The scale-up was informed by two previous pieces of research. A 2022 mailer trial looked at how different marketing strategies encouraged the adoption of an evidence-based programme by schools. An interim report from the first phase of the research identified that School Leads, TLC Leaders and classroom teachers made a range of adaptations to the programme due to contextual factors including other CPD priorities, the ongoing impact of Covid, the school’s leadership and culture, and specific characteristics of a school’s staff and pupils. The research also identified a lack of data on mentors and systems to ensure that the data collected was acted upon. EEF Summary
The programme was developed based on existing evidence that formative assessment can improve students’ learning. Many schools already prioritise formative assessment, but often report that it can be challenging to implement. EFA provides schools with a structured approach to developing their formative assessment practices. A previous EEF effectiveness trial in 140 schools had promising results, with students in the EFA schools making the equivalent of two months’ additional progress on their Attainment 8 GCSE scores. trials.title: Emotion Coaching – trial
trials.subtitle: Trial to test the impact of Emotion Coaching, a four-step relational approach aimed at developing personal, social and emotional skills, including self-regulation, in children.
trials.organisation: Emotion Coaching UK and Norland College

sections.heading: The project
sections.text: Emotion Coaching is a professional development programme for early years practitioners that aims to help 3 – 4‑year-old children develop self-regulation.It supports practitioners to use a four-step co-regulation framework to respond to children experiencing heightened emotions. The framework aims to help them understand their feelings, why they occur and how to manage them.The programme also aims to develop practitioners’ ability to model emotional awareness and regulation, and to create learning environments that support children’s Personal, Social and Emotional Development (PSED).
sections.html:
Emotion Coaching is a professional development programme for early years practitioners that aims to help 3 – 4‑year-old children develop self-regulation.

It supports practitioners to use a four-step co-regulation framework to respond to children experiencing heightened emotions. The framework aims to help them understand their feelings, why they occur and how to manage them.

The programme also aims to develop practitioners’ ability to model emotional awareness and regulation, and to create learning environments that support children’s Personal, Social and Emotional Development (PSED).

sections.heading: EEF summary
sections.text: As part of the Department for Education’s’ (DFE) Early Years Recovery Programme, the EEF worked with Stronger Practice Hubs (SPHs) across England to fund settings’ access to evidence-informed programmes and study the programme’s influence on practice and children’s outcomes. This initiative aimed to support education recovery following the pandemic, whilst also developing our understanding of effective professional development in the early years. Emotion Coaching was funded through this initiative.Originally developed as a parenting style clinically observed in the USA, Emotion Coaching has been adapted for use in education.A small number of studies in schools and settings in England provided some early evidence on the use of Emotion Coaching. Findings suggested that practitioners felt the approach was helpful and reported positive changes in their own practice and in children’s behaviour and emotional regulation. To strengthen the evidence of the impact of Emotion Coaching, an efficacy trial was completed in 2025. The evaluation found that Emotion Coaching had, on average:a small positive impact on children’s self-regulation (based on practitioner reports)a small positive effect on pro-social behaviours (based on practitioner reports)a moderate positive effect on adult’s meta-emotion philosophy (practitioners’ reactions, responses, and reasoning to emotions in themselves and others)This result has a three-padlock rating. This means we are moderately confident that the impact was due to the programme rather than other factors.The effects for children who were eligible for Early Years Pupil Premium (EYPP) were slightly larger, although these findings are less secure due to the smaller sample size for this group. As a result of this evidence, Emotion Coaching is one of the EEF’s Promising Programmes. The EEF is discussing next steps for a potential further evaluation of Emotion Coaching through a larger effectiveness trial. This would allow us to robustly test the impact of the programme for an EYPP sub-group at scale.
sections.html:
As part of the Department for Education’s’ (DFE) Early Years Recovery Programme, the EEF worked with Stronger Practice Hubs (SPHs) across England to fund settings’ access to evidence-informed programmes and study the programme’s influence on practice and children’s outcomes. This initiative aimed to support education recovery following the pandemic, whilst also developing our understanding of effective professional development in the early years. Emotion Coaching was funded through this initiative.

Originally developed as a parenting style clinically observed in the USA, Emotion Coaching has been adapted for use in education.

A small number of studies in schools and settings in England provided some early evidence on the use of Emotion Coaching. Findings suggested that practitioners felt the approach was helpful and reported positive changes in their own practice and in children’s behaviour and emotional regulation.

To strengthen the evidence of the impact of Emotion Coaching, an efficacy trial was completed in 2025.

The evaluation found that Emotion Coaching had, on average:

  • a small positive impact on children’s self-regulation (based on practitioner reports)
  • a small positive effect on pro-social behaviours (based on practitioner reports)
  • a moderate positive effect on adult’s meta-emotion philosophy (practitioners’ reactions, responses, and reasoning to emotions in themselves and others)

This result has a three-padlock rating. This means we are moderately confident that the impact was due to the programme rather than other factors.

The effects for children who were eligible for Early Years Pupil Premium (EYPP) were slightly larger, although these findings are less secure due to the smaller sample size for this group.

As a result of this evidence, Emotion Coaching is one of the EEF’s Promising Programmes. The EEF is discussing next steps for a potential further evaluation of Emotion Coaching through a larger effectiveness trial. This would allow us to robustly test the impact of the programme for an EYPP sub-group at scale.

sections.heading: Could I implement this in my school?
sections.text: Between two and four practitioners from each setting attended two days of online training, followed by three two-hour online workshops over the next three months. These practitioners were expected to share their learning with colleagues and support wider adoption of Emotion Coaching across the setting, using training materials, including activity handouts and pocket guides to embed the approach in everyday interactions with children. Overall, practitioners viewed Emotion Coaching positively and believed it could be adapted to different educational settings. Practitioner feedback suggested that implementation was strengthened by leadership support, opportunities for staff to share learning, and embedding Emotion Coaching within everyday routines and setting policies. However, implementation may be challenging if staff do not have enough time, training, or resources to use the approach consistently. Differences in children’s responsiveness, daily routines, and approaches between school and home may also affect how effectively the programme is delivered.It’s worth noting while the evaluation found a small positive impact on children’s self-regulation, practitioner views on implementation and the theory of change support that the implementation window for the programme might have been too short.Future evaluations may want to look at a longer implementation period to explore whether the practitioner level changes observed in this evaluation translate into larger, more reliably detected child outcomes over a more sustained period of implementation.Emotion Coaching is commercially available for educators and childcare providers.
sections.html:
Between two and four practitioners from each setting attended two days of online training, followed by three two-hour online workshops over the next three months. These practitioners were expected to share their learning with colleagues and support wider adoption of Emotion Coaching across the setting, using training materials, including activity handouts and pocket guides to embed the approach in everyday interactions with children.

Overall, practitioners viewed Emotion Coaching positively and believed it could be adapted to different educational settings. Practitioner feedback suggested that implementation was strengthened by leadership support, opportunities for staff to share learning, and embedding Emotion Coaching within everyday routines and setting policies. However, implementation may be challenging if staff do not have enough time, training, or resources to use the approach consistently. Differences in children’s responsiveness, daily routines, and approaches between school and home may also affect how effectively the programme is delivered.

It’s worth noting while the evaluation found a small positive impact on children’s self-regulation, practitioner views on implementation and the theory of change support that the implementation window for the programme might have been too short.

Future evaluations may want to look at a longer implementation period to explore whether the practitioner level changes observed in this evaluation translate into larger, more reliably detected child outcomes over a more sustained period of implementation.

Emotion Coaching is commercially available for educators and childcare providers.

sections.heading: How much will it cost?
sections.text: The average cost of Emotion Coaching was around £418.30 per setting and £16.70 per child per year, when averaged over three years, making it a very low-cost programme.

trials.title: FFT Reciprocal Reading – second trial
trials.subtitle: Trial to test the impact of Reciprocal Reading, a 12-week, targeted, structured approach to teaching reading comprehension.

sections.heading: The project
sections.text: Reciprocal Reading is a structured, discussion-based approach to the teaching of reading comprehension designed and delivered by FFT. This intervention is designed for pupils who read words accurately but often struggle to understand the meaning of what they read. It aims to develop pupils’ understanding of a text through the application of four strategies – predicting, clarifying, questioning, and summarising – used repeatedly on small sections of the text, to deal with comprehension difficulties as they emerge. The intervention is delivered by trained teachers and TAs for two 20 – 30-minute sessions per week, for a minimum of 12 weeks, to pupils in Years 5 and 6. Through repeated use of these strategies, readers become more confident in dealing with misunderstandings and start to apply the strategies to their own independent reading.
sections.html: Reciprocal Reading is a structured, discussion-based approach to the teaching of reading comprehension designed and delivered by FFT. This intervention is designed for pupils who read words accurately but often struggle to understand the meaning of what they read. It aims to develop pupils’ understanding of a text through the application of four strategies – predicting, clarifying, questioning, and summarising – used repeatedly on small sections of the text, to deal with comprehension difficulties as they emerge. The intervention is delivered by trained teachers and TAs for two 20 – 30-minute sessions per week, for a minimum of 12 weeks, to pupils in Years 5 and 6. Through repeated use of these strategies, readers become more confident in dealing with misunderstandings and start to apply the strategies to their own independent reading.

sections.heading: EEF summary
sections.text: The Reciprocal Reading effectiveness trial was funded through the Department of Education’s Accelerator Fund, which supports programmes that aim to improve pupil attainment. An earlier efficacy trial, funded by the EEF, tested FFT’s Reciprocal Reading programme in 98 schools with 5,222 pupils, using a targeted approach in Year 4 and a targeted approach for struggling readers in Years 5 and 6. The evaluation found that pupils in the targeted intervention made an average of two months’ additional progress in reading comprehension and overall reading compared to the control group, with even greater benefits for children eligible for free school meals. In the subsequent effectiveness trial, pupils made an average of one month’s additional progress in reading than the control group, with the potential gains of up to two months. Analysis also indicated improvements in reading accuracy and sentence-level comprehension, though not in passage comprehension, the programme’s main target. It is important to note that pupils who received at least 20 sessions over 12 weeks made roughly two months more progress than the average intervention pupil, suggesting that the intensity of the programme influences outcomes. Teachers reported substantial increases in confidence, understanding of key concepts, and practical knowledge following training, which was delivered with high levels of quality and attendance. Pupil engagement was consistently high, with the discussion-based format making reading feel more enjoyable and less like a task. The programme appeared to be more effective where pupils had strong prior reading skills and high engagement, and weaker where language or home factors posed barriers. While many pupils eligible for free school meals benefited, analysis indicated that these pupils made no additional month’s progress compared to the control group. Many control schools offered alternative reading interventions, which may have reduced the difference in outcomes and contributed to smaller overall impact in the trial.

trials.results_text:
EEF summary
The Reciprocal Reading effectiveness trial was funded through the Department of Education’s Accelerator Fund, which supports programmes that aim to improve pupil attainment. An earlier efficacy trial, funded by the EEF, tested FFT’s Reciprocal Reading programme in 98 schools with 5,222 pupils, using a targeted approach in Year 4 and a targeted approach for struggling readers in Years 5 and 6. The evaluation found that pupils in the targeted intervention made an average of two months’ additional progress in reading comprehension and overall reading compared to the control group, with even greater benefits for children eligible for free school meals. In the subsequent effectiveness trial, pupils made an average of one month’s additional progress in reading than the control group, with the potential gains of up to two months. Analysis also indicated improvements in reading accuracy and sentence-level comprehension, though not in passage comprehension, the programme’s main target. It is important to note that pupils who received at least 20 sessions over 12 weeks made roughly two months more progress than the average intervention pupil, suggesting that the intensity of the programme influences outcomes. Teachers reported substantial increases in confidence, understanding of key concepts, and practical knowledge following training, which was delivered with high levels of quality and attendance. Pupil engagement was consistently high, with the discussion-based format making reading feel more enjoyable and less like a task. The programme appeared to be more effective where pupils had strong prior reading skills and high engagement, and weaker where language or home factors posed barriers. While many pupils eligible for free school meals benefited, analysis indicated that these pupils made no additional month’s progress compared to the control group. Many control schools offered alternative reading interventions, which may have reduced the difference in outcomes and contributed to smaller overall impact in the trial.

trials.title: Focus4TAPS – first trial
trials.subtitle: Focus4TAPS is a CPD programme designed to support teachers to improve their teaching and assessment of science in primary schools.

sections.heading: The project
sections.text: The Focus4TAPS programme aims to improve science attainment of pupils, by improving teaching approaches and assessment in science. The course supports teachers to use assessment for learning in their classrooms, with a particular focus on assessing practical inquiry tasks to help pupils develop scientific reasoning skills and the use of self and peer-assessment to develop pupils’ metacognitive skills. The training provides resources and activities for teachers to use, however teachers are also encouraged to apply the principles to their own planning, so that the approaches become embedded in their teaching.
sections.html: The Focus4TAPS programme aims to improve science attainment of pupils, by improving teaching approaches and assessment in science. The course supports teachers to use assessment for learning in their classrooms, with a particular focus on assessing practical inquiry tasks to help pupils develop scientific reasoning skills and the use of self and peer-assessment to develop pupils’ metacognitive skills. The training provides resources and activities for teachers to use, however teachers are also encouraged to apply the principles to their own planning, so that the approaches become embedded in their teaching.

sections.heading: EEF summary
sections.text: As part of the Improving Science Education round, the EEF partnered with Wellcome to test projects that aimed to improve science attainment. Focus4TAPS was funded as part of that round.Wider evidence demonstrates the importance of formative use of assessment, an area that teachers find difficult to implement. The Teacher Assessment in Primary Science (TAPS) team had developed and piloted the resources and approach over several years, putting into practice a ​‘formative to summative’ model of assessment originally proposed by the Nuffield Foundation. TAPS research and development was funded by the Primary Science Teaching Trust. That development included qualitative research that suggested teachers did effectively improve their assessments following TAPS training, and increased their use of practical activities in science.This efficacy trial found that children in Focus4TAPS schools made, on average, the equivalent of two additional months’ progress in science compared to children in other schools. This result has a high security rating: 4 out of 5 on the EEF padlock scale. The evaluation also found a similar positive effect for children eligible for free school meals.The process evaluation found that the programme ran as expected, with 80% of teachers attending the minimum number of training sessions and 63% of teachers conducting at least four ​‘Focused Assessment’ lessons using Focus4TAPS materials. Greater compliance with the programme (for example, attending more training sessions and conducting more lessons) was associated with higher science test scores. The teachers in the intervention group reported, on average, higher confidence than those in the control group for many aspects of teaching and assessing science.This project and its evaluation were affected by the 2020 and 2021 partial school closures caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The trial originally started in 2019/20 but had to stop due to partial school closures, and was restarted with a new cohort of pupils in 2020/2021.As a result of these encouraging results, the EEF is conducting a larger effectiveness trial of Focus4TAPS delivered under everyday conditions.
sections.html:
As part of the Improving Science Education round, the EEF partnered with Wellcome to test projects that aimed to improve science attainment. Focus4TAPS was funded as part of that round.

Wider evidence demonstrates the importance of formative use of assessment, an area that teachers find difficult to implement. The Teacher Assessment in Primary Science (TAPS) team had developed and piloted the resources and approach over several years, putting into practice a ​‘formative to summative’ model of assessment originally proposed by the Nuffield Foundation. TAPS research and development was funded by the Primary Science Teaching Trust. That development included qualitative research that suggested teachers did effectively improve their assessments following TAPS training, and increased their use of practical activities in science.

This efficacy trial found that children in Focus4TAPS schools made, on average, the equivalent of two additional months’ progress in science compared to children in other schools. This result has a high security rating: 4 out of 5 on the EEF padlock scale. The evaluation also found a similar positive effect for children eligible for free school meals.

The process evaluation found that the programme ran as expected, with 80% of teachers attending the minimum number of training sessions and 63% of teachers conducting at least four ​‘Focused Assessment’ lessons using Focus4TAPS materials. Greater compliance with the programme (for example, attending more training sessions and conducting more lessons) was associated with higher science test scores. The teachers in the intervention group reported, on average, higher confidence than those in the control group for many aspects of teaching and assessing science.

This project and its evaluation were affected by the 2020 and 2021 partial school closures caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The trial originally started in 2019/20 but had to stop due to partial school closures, and was restarted with a new cohort of pupils in 2020/2021.

As a result of these encouraging results, the EEF is conducting a larger effectiveness trial of Focus4TAPS delivered under everyday conditions.

sections.heading: Could I implement this in my school?
sections.text: Typically the programme involves three days of PD, with in-school tasks in between, over the course of an academic year. Teachers meet in groups for the PD days. For this trial, due to COVID-19, the training was delivered remotely in six sessions spread over the year.Teachers are provided with example plans and activities for use in their classrooms. They are expected to select five TAPS plans from the bank of over 40 to carry out as gap tasks during the year, using largely everyday materials which will be found in school.The approach is implemented within the normal class science lessons. Since the approach is designed to modify teaching practice within lessons, this should not result in significant changes in the amount of science taught, unless the school is currently teaching less than the recommended two hours per week.The open-access resources are available from the PSTT website: https://pstt.org.uk/resources/curriculum-materials/assessment

sections.heading: How much will it cost?
sections.text: The average cost of the Focus4TAPS programme was around £1,355 per school over three years, or £19 per pupil per year when averaged over three years.The cost is based on 15 hours of teaching cover for a Year 5 teacher, 15 hours of teaching cover for a science leader, and £150.00 for online training costs, all occurring within the first year as start-up costs. The cost calculations also assume one Year 5 class of 24 pupils is involved in the intervention each year.

trials.subtitle: A professional development programme designed to improve the teaching and assessment of science in primary schools.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Focus4TAPS (Focus for Teaching Assessment of Primary Science) is a professional development programme that aims to improve primary pupils’ science attainment, by helping teachers improve the way they teach and assess science. The programme focuses on helping pupils develop science thinking, including scientific enquiry and reasoning skills, by encouraging them to investigate questions, collect and interpret evidence, and use self- and peer- assessment.Two teachers from each school attend three days of in-person professional development training and complete in-school tasks during their normal class science lessons between training sessions. They also have access to lessons plans, classroom activities, and curriculum and assessment materials on the Primary Science Teaching Trust website. This evaluation tested whether the programme improved pupils’ science attainment when delivered at scale, compared with usual Year 5 science teaching practice. It also explored whether pupils felt more confident in science, enjoyed science more, and were more interested in the subject.The programme focuses on the Working Scientifically principles in the English National Curriculum, which help pupils develop scientific enquiry skills and apply them in practical science lessons.It was tested through a large randomised controlled trial, under everyday conditions.
sections.html:
Focus4TAPS (Focus for Teaching Assessment of Primary Science) is a professional development programme that aims to improve primary pupils’ science attainment, by helping teachers improve the way they teach and assess science.

The programme focuses on helping pupils develop science thinking, including scientific enquiry and reasoning skills, by encouraging them to investigate questions, collect and interpret evidence, and use self- and peer- assessment.

Two teachers from each school attend three days of in-person professional development training and complete in-school tasks during their normal class science lessons between training sessions. They also have access to lessons plans, classroom activities, and curriculum and assessment materials on the Primary Science Teaching Trust website.

This evaluation tested whether the programme improved pupils’ science attainment when delivered at scale, compared with usual Year 5 science teaching practice. It also explored whether pupils felt more confident in science, enjoyed science more, and were more interested in the subject.

The programme focuses on the Working Scientifically principles in the English National Curriculum, which help pupils develop scientific enquiry skills and apply them in practical science lessons.

It was tested through a large randomised controlled trial, under everyday conditions.

sections.heading: Why did the EEF fund this project?
sections.text: Science is a core subject in the English primary curriculum. The State of Primary Science in the UK report found that, since 2017, more schools have a designated science lead and that weekly science provision is more common. However, it also found that teachers’ confidence, access to support, and access to subject-specific training have declined. At Key Stage 2, primary science attainment is assessed through teacher assessment rather than formal external tests. This highlights the importance of having a skilled and confident workforce to teach and assess science effectively.A previous EEF trial found that Focus4TAPs improved pupils’ science attainment by the equivalent of two additional months’ progress. Following these encouraging results, this trial tested whether the programme could achieve similar results when delivered at scale, using a scalable version of the training and resources across a larger number of schools.
sections.html:
Science is a core subject in the English primary curriculum. The State of Primary Science in the UK report found that, since 2017, more schools have a designated science lead and that weekly science provision is more common. However, it also found that teachers’ confidence, access to support, and access to subject-specific training have declined.

At Key Stage 2, primary science attainment is assessed through teacher assessment rather than formal external tests. This highlights the importance of having a skilled and confident workforce to teach and assess science effectively.

A previous EEF trial found that Focus4TAPs improved pupils’ science attainment by the equivalent of two additional months’ progress. Following these encouraging results, this trial tested whether the programme could achieve similar results when delivered at scale, using a scalable version of the training and resources across a larger number of schools.

sections.heading: What did the evaluation find?
sections.text: Pupils in Focus4TAPS schools made no additional months’ progress in science, on average, compared with pupils in schools delivering usual science teaching. This finding has a moderate to high security rating, which means we have a good level of confidence in it.Pupils eligible for Free School Meals made the equivalent of one additional month’s progress in science, on average, compared with similar pupils in schools delivering usual practice. This finding should be interpreted more cautiously because it is based on a smaller group of pupils so we cannot be as confident that it was a direct result of the programme.The evaluation found positive effects on all pupils’ attitudes and beliefs about science. Lesson observations in Focus4TAPS schools showed that pupils took greater ownership of their learning. This included planning parts of investigations, selecting variables, and recording their own results.Teachers reported that the approach supported a positive classroom culture and engagement with scientific investigation. They also said that practical activities were particularly inclusive for pupils who were less confident in science.Teachers reported increased confidence in teaching science, particularly in relation to using formative assessment and developing pupils’ Working Scientifically skills. The implementation and process evaluation found that the Focus4TAPS training was delivered largely as intended. Where adaptations were made, these were consistent with the programme guidance.Some elements of the Focus4TAPS approach were similar to practices already used in schools. Some schools were also already using Primary Science Teaching Trust resources before the trial. This may have reduced the distinctiveness of Focus4TAPS relative to usual teaching practices.
sections.html:
• Pupils in Focus4TAPS schools made no additional months’ progress in science, on average, compared with pupils in schools delivering usual science teaching. This finding has a moderate to high security rating, which means we have a good level of confidence in it.
  • Pupils eligible for Free School Meals made the equivalent of one additional month’s progress in science, on average, compared with similar pupils in schools delivering usual practice. This finding should be interpreted more cautiously because it is based on a smaller group of pupils so we cannot be as confident that it was a direct result of the programme.
  • The evaluation found positive effects on all pupils’ attitudes and beliefs about science. Lesson observations in Focus4TAPS schools showed that pupils took greater ownership of their learning. This included planning parts of investigations, selecting variables, and recording their own results.
  • Teachers reported that the approach supported a positive classroom culture and engagement with scientific investigation. They also said that practical activities were particularly inclusive for pupils who were less confident in science.
  • Teachers reported increased confidence in teaching science, particularly in relation to using formative assessment and developing pupils’ Working Scientifically skills. The implementation and process evaluation found that the Focus4TAPS training was delivered largely as intended. Where adaptations were made, these were consistent with the programme guidance.
  • Some elements of the Focus4TAPS approach were similar to practices already used in schools. Some schools were also already using Primary Science Teaching Trust resources before the trial. This may have reduced the distinctiveness of Focus4TAPS relative to usual teaching practices.

sections.heading: How should I interpret these findings?
sections.text: Overall, the trial does not provide strong evidence that Focus4TAPS improves science attainment more than usual science teaching. However, this should be interpreted cautiously because attainment data was not available for just over one in five pupils (21.1%). This means the results may not fully represent all the pupils who took part in the trial. The findings are inconclusive and included effects that both indicated positive improvements in science attainment, and negative effects.There was some encouraging evidence that Focus4TAPS influenced classroom practice. Teachers engaged positively with the training, and lesson observations showed that pupils took greater ownership of their learning, including planning parts of investigations, selecting variables and recording their own results. However, these changes in classroom practice did not translate into consistent improvements in science attainment within the academic year of the trial.The earlier positive trial results suggest that the approach may be effective in some circumstances. Schools considering Focus4TAPS should consider the evidence alongside their own context and whether they have the capacity to deliver the programme, including releasing two teachers for professional development and providing sufficient time for science teaching.

sections.heading: Could I implement this in my setting?
sections.text: To deliver Focus4TAPS, schools need to release two teachers, including the science lead, for three days of in-person professional development during the academic year. If teachers are unable to attend a live session, they can watch a summary video to catch up. All classroom materials are also available online.Between training sessions, teachers deliver at least five lessons using the Focus4TAPS approach during their usual science teaching time. They can adapt lessons to meet the specific needs of pupils in their class, using the programme’s lesson plans and resources for support. Focus4TAPS is not intended to increase the amount of time schools spend teaching science, unless they currently teach less than the recommended two hours per week.

trials.title: Improving Numeracy and Literacy in Key Stage 1 – trial
trials.subtitle: Improving pupils’ numeracy and literacy through two programmes: ​‘Mathematical Reasoning’ and ​‘Literacy and Morphemes’

sections.heading: EEF Summary
sections.text: Previous studies suggested both programmes offered affordable approaches to improving pupil outcomes. Based on this, the EEF funded a trial (Improving Literacy and Numeracy in KS1) to test the impact of the two programmes under developer-led conditions. Pupils receiving Mathematical Reasoning made an additional three months’ progress in maths compared to other pupils in comparison schools. There was no evidence that Literacy and Morphemes improved spelling or reading outcomes.The EEF then funded a follow-up evaluation which examined the impact of a scalable version of Mathematical Reasoning in a larger number of schools and with less involvement from the original developer (co-funded by the Worshipful Company of Actuaries). The National Centre for Excellence in the Teaching of Mathematics (NCETM) helped to develop the training model, and coordinated its delivery through its national network of ​‘Maths Hubs’ (partnerships of schools focused on maths education). In this second, larger trial, pupils who received Mathematical Reasoning made the equivalent of one additional month’s progress in maths, on average, compared to other children.There are some differences between the two projects which may explain the smaller impact in the second trial. First, it used a different delivery model. Rather than doing the teaching training directly, the programme developers (the University of Oxford) trained Maths Hub teachers who then delivered the teacher training to participating schools. This may have affected how faithfully the programme was delivered in the classroom. Also, although a precise comparison is difficult, there was evidence that the comparison schools in the second trial were more likely than in the first trial to provide alternative support for children’s reasoning in maths. This may have reduced the difference seen between Mathematical Reasoning pupils and other pupils.Together, these trials provide evidence for the effectiveness of Mathematical Reasoning. The project will remain on the EEF’s Promising Programmes list and we will explore the potential for bringing it to more schools.

sections.heading: Evaluation Conclusions
sections.text: This evaluation provided evidence that the Mathematics and Reasoning programme had a positive impact on pupils’ numeracy ability equating to three additional months’ progress.There was no evidence to suggest that the Literacy and Morphemes programme had an impact on pupils’ literacy ability overall.There was an association between greater use of the accompanying computer games and greater impact in the numeracy intervention, suggesting the computer games were important to successful implementation.All teachers were able to implement the programmes, but most agreed there was too much content to deliver in one hour per week and so made various adaptations to their delivery of the programme. In future trials of the programmes, teachers should be permitted to use and integrate the materials in their own way, as they would in a normal teaching situation.A future trial could evaluate the programmes at scale in more than one location. When drawing up plans for bringing the programmes to scale, the Oxford team should consider whether training and ongoing technical support could be delivered remotely, rather than in person.

EEF Summary
Previous studies suggested both programmes offered affordable approaches to improving pupil outcomes. Based on this, the EEF funded a trial (Improving Literacy and Numeracy in KS1) to test the impact of the two programmes under developer-led conditions. Pupils receiving Mathematical Reasoning made an additional three months’ progress in maths compared to other pupils in comparison schools. The National Centre for Excellence in the Teaching of Mathematics (NCETM) helped to develop the training model, and coordinated its delivery through its national network of ​‘Maths Hubs’ (partnerships of schools focused on maths education). In this second, larger trial, pupils who received Mathematical Reasoning made the equivalent of one additional month’s progress in maths, on average, compared to other children.There are some differences between the two projects which may explain the smaller impact in the second trial. Rather than doing the teaching training directly, the programme developers (the University of Oxford) trained Maths Hub teachers who then delivered the teacher training to participating schools. Also, although a precise comparison is difficult, there was evidence that the comparison schools in the second trial were more likely than in the first trial to provide alternative support for children’s reasoning in maths. In future trials of the programmes, teachers should be permitted to use and integrate the materials in their own way, as they would in a normal teaching situation.A future trial could evaluate the programmes at scale in more than one location. trials.title: Lexia® Core5® Reading (first trial)
trials.subtitle: Testing a computer-based reading programme.

sections.heading: EEF summary
sections.text: Research has identified remedial and tutorial use of technology as being particularly practical for lower attaining pupils, those with special educational needs or those from disadvantaged backgrounds in providing intensive support to enable them to catch up with their peers. Technology can be particularly useful in personalising learning to match pupils’ individual abilities and needs given the potential for such programmes to adapt and focus on the child’s learning needs.Lexia® Core® Reading is currently used in over 3,000 schools in the UK. Previous research on Lexia in the US and UK found promising results. This trial is the first opportunity to evaluate the programme using a large-scale RCT within the UK context, using outcomes that measure all-round reading ability. The evaluation also measured the individual skills that compose​‘reading skills’, which allows for comparison with previous studies and to identify any areas of strength or weakness in the programme in terms of enhancing children’s reading development.Our trial of Lexia involved 697 pupils across 57 schools. The independent evaluation found that children offered Lexia made the equivalent of one additional months’ progress in reading, on average, compared to other children. These results have a high security rating: four out of five on the EEF padlock scale. Children eligible for Free School Meals (FSM) who were offered Lexia made, on average, the equivalent of two additional months’ progress in reading compared to other children eligible for FSM.1The evaluation also found that the programme had a positive effect on skills that are important for further literacy development.This was a promising result, therefore Lexia is currently being evaluated at effectiveness level by the EEF, to assess the impact when delivered to a larger number of settings under everyday conditions.
sections.html:
Research has identified remedial and tutorial use of technology as being particularly practical for lower attaining pupils, those with special educational needs or those from disadvantaged backgrounds in providing intensive support to enable them to catch up with their peers. Technology can be particularly useful in personalising learning to match pupils’ individual abilities and needs given the potential for such programmes to adapt and focus on the child’s learning needs.

Lexia® Core® Reading is currently used in over 3,000 schools in the UK. Previous research on Lexia in the US and UK found promising results. This trial is the first opportunity to evaluate the programme using a large-scale RCT within the UK context, using outcomes that measure all-round reading ability. The evaluation also measured the individual skills that compose​‘reading skills’, which allows for comparison with previous studies and to identify any areas of strength or weakness in the programme in terms of enhancing children’s reading development.

Our trial of Lexia involved 697 pupils across 57 schools. The independent evaluation found that children offered Lexia made the equivalent of one additional months’ progress in reading, on average, compared to other children. These results have a high security rating: four out of five on the EEF padlock scale. Children eligible for Free School Meals (FSM) who were offered Lexia made, on average, the equivalent of two additional months’ progress in reading compared to other children eligible for FSM.1

The evaluation also found that the programme had a positive effect on skills that are important for further literacy development.

This was a promising result, therefore Lexia is currently being evaluated at effectiveness level by the EEF, to assess the impact when delivered to a larger number of settings under everyday conditions.

sections.html:
1. Children offered Lexia made the equivalent of one additional months’ progress in reading, on average, compared to other children. This result has a high security rating.
  2. Exploratory analysis suggests that children offered Lexia made the equivalent of two additional months’ progress in word recognition and decoding skills and one additional month of progress in reading fluency and comprehension skills, on average, compared to other children. Children offered Lexia made, on average, no additional progress in Key Stage 1 national test reading raw scores compared to other children.
  3. Children eligible for Free School Meals (FSM) who were offered Lexia made, on average, the equivalent of two additional months’ progress in reading compared to other children eligible for FSM. However, this result has high statistical uncertainty.
  4. Implementation fidelity was high. Most schools incorporated Lexia into their routine so that pupils received the normal provision for struggling readers as well as this intervention. Over three-quarters of survey respondents were satisfied with the access to the online activities, support provided, and the usefulness of the reports.
  5. Most pupils managed to work independently with little scaffolding from teaching assistants. However, teachers and teaching assistants felt that Lexia was unsuitable for a small number of pupils, especially those with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities and those whose reading level was very low.
  6. An alternative analysis shows a slightly higher impact of two months’ progress in reading for all pupils and three months’ progress in reading for FSM pupils (exploratory analysis). This analysis was communicated in the previous version of the evaluation report (see Appendix C) but has been superseded in this evaluation report by the analysis pre-specified before the analysis was conducted. 

Key Conclusions presented in the previous version of this report (published February 2022) can be found in Appendix C of the evaluation report.

sections.heading: Were the schools in the trial similar to my school?
sections.text: There were 57 schools involved in the trial.Schools needed to have approximately 50 pupils per year group, and be able to provide the necessary IT technology required in order to support the intervention.Schools were based in the regions of the North East, Yorkshire and Humber, Wiltshire, Lancashire and Greater London.92% of schools had an Ofsted rating of ​“Outstanding” or ​“Good”.On average, 33% of pupils in schools in the trial were eligible for Free School Meals.
sections.html:
• There were 57 schools involved in the trial.
  • Schools needed to have approximately 50 pupils per year group, and be able to provide the necessary IT technology required in order to support the intervention.
  • Schools were based in the regions of the North East, Yorkshire and Humber, Wiltshire, Lancashire and Greater London.
  • 92% of schools had an Ofsted rating of ​“Outstanding” or ​“Good”.
  • On average, 33% of pupils in schools in the trial were eligible for Free School Meals.

sections.heading: How was this implemented?
sections.text: LexiaUK provide software licences, online training and ongoing support.Lexia sessions require one device (tablet, laptop, PC, etc.) per child. In addition, most schools in the trial also provided one set of headphones per child. There were also some financial costs associated with printing paper-based resources.The additional time costs were for staff training, which involved three one-hour sessions, and delivery time for the facilitator (often a teaching assistant, although sometimes a teacher).
sections.html:
• LexiaUK provide software licences, online training and ongoing support.
  • Lexia sessions require one device (tablet, laptop, PC, etc.) per child. In addition, most schools in the trial also provided one set of headphones per child. There were also some financial costs associated with printing paper-based resources.
  • The additional time costs were for staff training, which involved three one-hour sessions, and delivery time for the facilitator (often a teaching assistant, although sometimes a teacher).

sections.heading: How much does it cost?
sections.text: The cost to schools of delivering the programme is very low: £41.00 per pupil per year, as averaged over three years. The cumulative cost to schools over a three-year period is £3,690. These estimates are based on one practitioner being trained per setting and delivering the programme to 30 pupils per year.

trials.title: Lexia® Core5® Reading (second trial)
trials.subtitle: A technology-led adaptive literacy programme that aims to improve struggling primary pupils’ reading outcomes by providing personalised practice and instruction.

sections.heading: Why did the EEF fund this project?
sections.text: A previous EEF efficacy trial found that Lexia® Core5® Reading improved children’s reading attainment by the equivalent of one additional month’s progress. These results have a high security rating: four out of five on the EEF padlock scale.Children eligible for free school meals (FSM) made two additional months’ progress, and all pupils gained an extra month in comprehension and fluency, skills important for later reading. Due to these promising results, the larger trial was designed to test Lexia at scale, in real-world conditions.
sections.html:
A previous EEF efficacy trial found that Lexia® Core5® Reading improved children’s reading attainment by the equivalent of one additional month’s progress. These results have a high security rating: four out of five on the EEF padlock scale.

Children eligible for free school meals (FSM) made two additional months’ progress, and all pupils gained an extra month in comprehension and fluency, skills important for later reading.

Due to these promising results, the larger trial was designed to test Lexia at scale, in real-world conditions.

sections.heading: What did the evaluation find?
sections.text: Struggling readers in schools delivering Lexia made two additional months’ progress in reading, on average, compared with pupils of similar attainment in comparison schools. This finding has a high security rating, which means we have confidence in it.Struggling readers eligible for free school meals in schools delivering Lexia also made two additional months’ progress. However, this finding is less secure because it was based on a smaller group of pupils.The analysis also looked at the programme’s impact on different areas measured by the assessment. Pupils made two months’ additional progress in word identification, applying phonics and passage comprehension, but no additional progress was observed in oral fluency.The evaluation also found that pupils who used Lexia more than the minimum recommended amount tended to make greater progress.Further exploratory analysis suggested that pupils with stronger reading skills (although still classed as struggling readers by their schools) at the start of the trial, and those without special educational needs and disabilities, tended to make more progress than pupils who started out with weaker reading skills or who had these needs. These findings are based on smaller numbers of pupils and should be treated with caution.Exploratory analysis also suggested that struggling readers with English as an Additional Language (EAL) made three additional months’ progress in reading – more than struggling readers overall. However, small pupil numbers mean we cannot be confident that Lexia closes the gap for this group specifically.The implementation and process evaluation found that Lexia was relatively easy to deliver where schools already had the right technology in place (laptops, headphones and internet access), with strong training from Lexia and commitment from school staff helping delivery run smoothly.
sections.html:
• Struggling readers in schools delivering Lexia made two additional months’ progress in reading, on average, compared with pupils of similar attainment in comparison schools. This finding has a high security rating, which means we have confidence in it.
  • Struggling readers eligible for free school meals in schools delivering Lexia also made two additional months’ progress. However, this finding is less secure because it was based on a smaller group of pupils.
  • The analysis also looked at the programme’s impact on different areas measured by the assessment. Pupils made two months’ additional progress in word identification, applying phonics and passage comprehension, but no additional progress was observed in oral fluency.
  • The evaluation also found that pupils who used Lexia more than the minimum recommended amount tended to make greater progress.
  • Further exploratory analysis suggested that pupils with stronger reading skills (although still classed as struggling readers by their schools) at the start of the trial, and those without special educational needs and disabilities, tended to make more progress than pupils who started out with weaker reading skills or who had these needs. These findings are based on smaller numbers of pupils and should be treated with caution.
  • Exploratory analysis also suggested that struggling readers with English as an Additional Language (EAL) made three additional months’ progress in reading – more than struggling readers overall. However, small pupil numbers mean we cannot be confident that Lexia closes the gap for this group specifically.
  • The implementation and process evaluation found that Lexia was relatively easy to deliver where schools already had the right technology in place (laptops, headphones and internet access), with strong training from Lexia and commitment from school staff helping delivery run smoothly.

sections.heading: How should I interpret these findings?
sections.text: This evaluation provides strong evidence that Lexia® Core5® Reading helps Year 2 readers make faster progress through personalised online practice in phonics, fluency, vocabulary and comprehension, combined, alongside support from teachers and teaching assistants. The estimated impact on children eligible for free school meals was similar to the overall result, suggesting the programme could be a good investment for Pupil Premium spend. However, this finding is based on a smaller number of pupils and carries a lower security rating than the overall result. Overall, the positive findings and high security rating mean that schools should feel confident that Lexia is a credible option for supporting struggling readers in Year 2. Most schools found Lexia relatively straightforward to deliver, particularly where laptops, headphones and reliable internet were already available. Schools without this technology should factor in the time and investment needed to put it in place. Some findings, including those relating to pupils with SEND, EAL pupils, and pupils using Lexia beyond the minimum recommended amount, are based on smaller samples. Further research would help confirm whether these patterns hold.

sections.heading: Were the settings in the trial similar to mine?
sections.text: This evaluation involved 224 schools and 2,197 pupils across England.Schools were recruited nationwide across England, with recruitment done to maximise geographical spread.50% of schools were located in Education Investment Areas (EIAs) – educationally underperforming areas prioritised by the government for further support and funding.
sections.html:
• This evaluation involved 224 schools and 2,197 pupils across England.
  • Schools were recruited nationwide across England, with recruitment done to maximise geographical spread.
  • 50% of schools were located in Education Investment Areas (EIAs) – educationally underperforming areas prioritised by the government for further support and funding.

sections.heading: Could I implement this in my setting?
sections.text: To deliver Lexia® Core5® Reading, schools need access to computers and internet connection, as the programme is largely delivered online with the support of downloadable printable teacher resources.Lexia sessions require one device (tablet, laptop, PC, etc.) per child. Some schools reported additional purchases such as headphones.Teachers and TAs received three training sessions (1 hour and 15 minutes each) and ongoing support from Lexia throughout the programme.Staff who took part in the evaluation did not identify any major barriers to implementing the programme.
sections.html:
• To deliver Lexia® Core5® Reading, schools need access to computers and internet connection, as the programme is largely delivered online with the support of downloadable printable teacher resources.
  • Lexia sessions require one device (tablet, laptop, PC, etc.) per child. Some schools reported additional purchases such as headphones.
  • Teachers and TAs received three training sessions (1 hour and 15 minutes each) and ongoing support from Lexia throughout the programme.
  • Staff who took part in the evaluation did not identify any major barriers to implementing the programme.

sections.heading: How much will it cost?
sections.text: The average cost of implementing Lexia cost was £4,186 per school over three years, equivalent to £27.91 per pupil, per year.These costs include staff training, optional staff cover and optional programme materials.This programme is currently available to schools through LexiaUK.

Previous studies suggested both programmes offered affordable approaches to improving pupil outcomes. Based on this, the EEF funded a trial (Improving Literacy and Numeracy in KS1) to test the impact of the two programmes under developer-led conditions. Pupils receiving Mathematical Reasoning made an additional three months’ progress in maths compared to other pupils in comparison schools. There was no evidence that Literacy and Morphemes improved spelling or reading outcomes.

The EEF then funded a follow-up evaluation which examined the impact of a scalable version of Mathematical Reasoning in a larger number of schools and with less involvement from the original developer (co-funded by the Worshipful Company of Actuaries). The National Centre for Excellence in the Teaching of Mathematics (NCETM) helped to develop the training model, and coordinated its delivery through its national network of ​‘Maths Hubs’ (partnerships of schools focused on maths education). In this second, larger trial, pupils who received Mathematical Reasoning made the equivalent of one additional month’s progress in maths, on average, compared to other children.

Rather than doing the teaching training directly, the programme developers (the University of Oxford) trained Maths Hub teachers who then delivered the teacher training to participating schools. This may have affected how faithfully the programme was delivered in the classroom. Also, although a precise comparison is difficult, there was evidence that the comparison schools in the second trial were more likely than in the first trial to provide alternative support for children’s reasoning in maths. This may have reduced the difference seen between Mathematical Reasoning pupils and other pupils.

trials.title: Mathematical Reasoning – pilot
trials.subtitle: Pilot to assess the acceptability and feasibility of an online version of the Mathematical Reasoning teacher training programme.

sections.heading: EEF Summary
sections.text: Mathematical Reasoning is an established intervention which has shown promise in previous EEF evaluations. An efficacy trial found pupils made an additional three months’ progress compared to control schools. A subsequent effectiveness trial showed one month’s additional progress. To enable scalability while maintaining effectiveness, the developers created an online version of the teacher training. This pilot aimed to assess the acceptability and feasibility of this online training model. The online training was generally considered useful by teaching staff in preparing them to deliver the programme. Most of the surveyed teaching staff reported confidence in being able to use the programme following the initial online training, and subsequently conveyed confidence in being able to use the programme towards the end of the programme. The videos demonstrating classroom practice received the highest ratings for usefulness though some found the mathematical terminology covered to be challenging to understand. On average, teachers reported delivering 9 out of 12 teaching units after training, which is in line with the programme expectations. The online format offered flexibility and convenience, but some challenges included limited interaction and an understanding of the time commitments required to complete the training. Teacher Leaders, who were responsible for supporting the participating teachers, felt equipped for their role and demonstrated the ability to adapt their support as needed. The findings broadly support the theory of change that the online training can effectively prepare teachers to deliver the Mathematical Reasoning programme. While no fundamental barriers to scaling were reported, some refinements were suggested, such as providing more classroom practice videos and streamlining content. Further evaluation would be needed to assess the effectiveness of the full Mathematical Reasoning programme, containing this online mode of teacher training, on pupil attainment. The EEF is currently undertaking an effectiveness trial to assess the full impact of this programme when delivered at scale.

trials.title: Mathematical Reasoning (second effectiveness trial)
trials.subtitle: A maths programme that develops Year 2 pupils’ mathematical reasoning through teacher training, teaching assistant support, structured lessons, and computer games.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Mathematical Reasoning is a maths programme for Year 2 pupils developed by the University of Oxford. It aims to improve pupils’ maths attainment by promoting depth of knowledge, strengthening their mathematical reasoning, number sense, and quantitative reasoning.Over 12 to 15 weeks, teachers replace one maths lesson each week with structured sessions that combine whole-class teaching, group activities, and computer games.Teachers and teaching assistants complete online training and attend webinars before and during delivery.This evaluation tested whether the programme improved pupils’ maths attainment when delivered at scale, compared with usual Year 2 maths teaching practice.It was tested through a large randomised controlled trial, under everyday conditions.
sections.html:
Mathematical Reasoning is a maths programme for Year 2 pupils developed by the University of Oxford. It aims to improve pupils’ maths attainment by promoting depth of knowledge, strengthening their mathematical reasoning, number sense, and quantitative reasoning.

Over 12 to 15 weeks, teachers replace one maths lesson each week with structured sessions that combine whole-class teaching, group activities, and computer games.

Teachers and teaching assistants complete online training and attend webinars before and during delivery.

This evaluation tested whether the programme improved pupils’ maths attainment when delivered at scale, compared with usual Year 2 maths teaching practice.

It was tested through a large randomised controlled trial, under everyday conditions.

sections.heading: Why did the EEF fund this project?
sections.text: Strong maths foundations are associated with later educational success. Mathematical Reasoning was developed because research suggests that children’s understanding of quantitative reasoning and number sense predict later mathematics attainment. The EEF previously funded two randomised controlled trials of the programme. The first trial, conducted under ideal conditions, found an impact of three additional months’ progress. A second larger trial, conducted under everyday conditions found a smaller impact of one additional month’s progress.This second effectiveness trial tested whether an online training model, with modules delivered by the programme designers, improved implementation and retained more of the impact seen in the earlier efficacy trial.
sections.html:
Strong maths foundations are associated with later educational success. Mathematical Reasoning was developed because research suggests that children’s understanding of quantitative reasoning and number sense predict later mathematics attainment.
The EEF previously funded two randomised controlled trials of the programme. The first trial, conducted under ideal conditions, found an impact of three additional months’ progress. A second larger trial, conducted under everyday conditions found a smaller impact of one additional month’s progress.

This second effectiveness trial tested whether an online training model, with modules delivered by the programme designers, improved implementation and retained more of the impact seen in the earlier efficacy trial.

sections.heading: What did the evaluation find?
sections.text: Pupils in Mathematical Reasoning schools made the equivalent of one additional month of progress in maths, on average, compared with pupils in schools delivering usual practice. This finding has a high security rating, which means we have confidence in it.Pupils eligible for Free School Meals made the equivalent of two additional months of progress, on average, compared with similar pupils in schools delivering usual practice. This finding should be interpreted more cautiously because it is based on a smaller group of pupils.Exploratory analysis suggested that pupils with lower prior attainment may have benefited more than pupils with higher prior attainment.Teachers reported that the programme improved their understanding of and confidence in teaching mathematical reasoning. Most teachers also felt the programme had a positive impact on pupils’ mathematical reasoning, arithmetic skills, confidence, and enjoyment of maths.Teachers reported that support from teaching assistants during programme sessions was important for delivering the programme as intended. Some schools reported that the training requirements and demands of delivering the programme made it challenging to implement.
sections.html:
• Pupils in Mathematical Reasoning schools made the equivalent of one additional month of progress in maths, on average, compared with pupils in schools delivering usual practice. This finding has a high security rating, which means we have confidence in it.
  • Pupils eligible for Free School Meals made the equivalent of two additional months of progress, on average, compared with similar pupils in schools delivering usual practice. This finding should be interpreted more cautiously because it is based on a smaller group of pupils.
  • Exploratory analysis suggested that pupils with lower prior attainment may have benefited more than pupils with higher prior attainment.
  • Teachers reported that the programme improved their understanding of and confidence in teaching mathematical reasoning. Most teachers also felt the programme had a positive impact on pupils’ mathematical reasoning, arithmetic skills, confidence, and enjoyment of maths.
  • Teachers reported that support from teaching assistants during programme sessions was important for delivering the programme as intended. Some schools reported that the training requirements and demands of delivering the programme made it challenging to implement.

sections.heading: How should I interpret these findings?
sections.text: This evaluation provides strong evidence that Mathematical Reasoning can improve maths attainment for Year 2 pupils.The overall impact was modest but positive and was observed in a large trial conducted under everyday school conditions. The high security rating means we have confidence in the main finding.The programme appears particularly promising for pupils eligible for Free School Meals and pupils with lower prior attainment, although these findings are less secure than the overall result.The findings also suggest that implementation matters. Some schools did not always deliver the full programme as intended, particularly where time, staffing, or teaching assistant capacity were limited. Despite these challenges, the programme still produced a positive overall impact.
sections.html:
• This evaluation provides strong evidence that Mathematical Reasoning can improve maths attainment for Year 2 pupils.
  • The overall impact was modest but positive and was observed in a large trial conducted under everyday school conditions. The high security rating means we have confidence in the main finding.
  • The programme appears particularly promising for pupils eligible for Free School Meals and pupils with lower prior attainment, although these findings are less secure than the overall result.
